en: Having prostrated before the eternal Brahman, who possesses the knowledge of the fifty sounds and objects beyond the senses,
I shall explain the characteristics of the vowels for the *Taittirīyapada* and other texts. 1.
The acute (udātta) and the grave (anudātta) are the two natural accents (svarau) of the phonemes;
the circumflex (svarita) is said to be of two kinds, as well as the sustained (dhṛta) and the combined (sāṃhita).
A "similar accent" (tulyasvara) occurs when the meaning is identical, even when there is a distinction in the case-endings (supām) within a word.

Even when there is a double *avagraha*, the same rule applies; likewise, when a portion of the suffix *iṅ* arises from a case-ending, there shall be only one acute (*udātta*) accent. Even in the case of *īṅ* within a single word, it is naturally so;
furthermore, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is always acute at the end of a sentence, as in the examples "annānte" and "viṃdati."

This is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): the word *vāva* has two udātta accents; [the same applies to] *ad*, *asmai*, *pūrvam*, and *voḍhave*; and for words ending in *tavai*, even when followed by *īṅya*, there is the *baṃbā* accentuation, as is heard in the case of *viśvavayaḥ*. 5.
Words such as *vanaspati* and others, when not used in the vocative case or as secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), [retain their original accent];
likewise do *bṛhaspati*, even in a compound, as well as *śunaḥśepa* and *śacīpati*.
Furthermore, *agnāviṣṇū*, *indrāviṣṇū*, *naktoṣāsau*, and *uṣāsānaktā* [are similarly accented].
Śaṇḍa, Marka, Avidhma, Barhis, Nābhānediṣṭha, Agni, and Soma;
Śunasīra, Narāśaṃsa, Tanūnaptra, Tanūnapāt, Dyāvāpṛthivī, the Śukra and Manthin vessels, and the Gāparūṣas. 7–8.

The three words ending with Varuṇa; the three words beginning with the terms Mitra, Agni, and Indra; the word *dvirūpa*; and the words *satra*, *ṛtu*, and those standing in the position of *prajā* and so forth [are unaccented].
In the word *yajñapati*, the *u* is udātta; in *agnā*, [the vowel] is udātta; and in *indrābṛhaspatiḥ*, [the first vowel is udātta].
Thus ends the extensive section on the acute accent (udātta). Now follows the exception regarding the equal tone (tulyasvara):
"The third vowel and those following it are unaccented (anudātta), provided they are not followed by a vowel of the same pitch as the preceding one. 10.

In words such as *gavādi*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and subsequent cases beginning with *apaḥ* have the acute accent on the first syllable; the word *kṛṣṇaḥ* is so when referring to a deer; and the group of words beginning with *pra*, excluding *abhi*, [have the acute accent on the first syllable].
Words ending in *an* or *as* have the acute accent on the final syllable; however, the word *brahman* does not [end with an acute accent] when it is in the neuter gender.

Then, "tad-ādy-ānaya" and "eta" are high-pitched (udātta); however, in cases such as "dvitīyam," "etat-ādiṣu," "meghyā," "kṣemyāya," and "gṛhyaye," the subsequent syllables are otherwise [low-pitched].
But those beginning with a long vowel, such as "āditya," "araṇya," and "āsura," have the final syllable high-pitched (antodātta).
The *havya* (oblation), the *veda*, and the *brāhmaṇa*; the sacrificial grass (*havistṛṇa*) and so forth;
the blind person (*andha*), the living being (*jantu*), and the unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) and so forth; likewise the wing (*pakṣa*), the shoulder (*skandha*), and the rule (*vidhi*).
In this same way, you are situated between two [states] like Aryaman, Āyu, and Pūrva.
The second section on "Equal Vowels" (tulyasvara) is completed.
Even when a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) results in an acute accent (*udātta*), the *avagraha* divisions remain unaccented (*anudātta*).
Furthermore, in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) and words ending in the suffix *-al*, the initial prefixes (*upasarga*)—such as *abhītvarīḥ*—remain unaccented.

Sprinkling for one who is looking on, offering, and the ointment for the journey; the sprinkling-vessel, the consecrated [animal], and the two Śruti texts; the examination, and also the calls (praiṣas) and the searches (meṣas);
"for the coming," and also "every day," "the devourer," and "the flesh-eater. 16–17.

"O Agni, you who are worthy of being eaten as an oblation, who are the consumer of darkness, who are the giver of wealth, who are the swift path to the bitter [remedy], who are the eater of food, and who are the one to whom the first portion of the offering belongs—O Agnidh, [I offer] for the sake of the words 'food' and 'eating,' for the sake of the oblation, for the sake of the self, and for the sake of the purpose of the one who bestows strength.
(18) "The offered and the unoffered, for the sake of the self, for that purpose, for the sake of the one who moves toward the goal. (19)
The *apombhana* verses and those following them are to be recited with a circumflex accent (*paridhi*) when introduced; likewise, all [the subsequent verses] are *anudātta*.
One should indeed utter "u," "svid," "īm," "ha smaiva," "vac," "vā," "ghas," "īm," "yā," and "yuṣmad" and "asmad" as "te," "mām," "it," "āvām," "naḥ," and "vaḥ" respectively. 20.

The substitution of *enad* for *enam* does not occur before *na*; in the Veda, the word *iṅgye* is also a finite verb (*tiṅpada*), and sometimes a finite verb form such as *avagau*, *hatasvaḥ*, or *kariti* is seen.
There are vocatives consisting of two syllables beginning with the words *idam* and *śabdaiḥ*.
The word *tvaḥ* is not [used] when it occurs within the same sentence as another referent, whether that be "on earth" (*pṛthivyām*) or "in the world" (*loke*).
When it functions as a pronoun, it is equal to *sarva*; likewise, it may stand at the end of a verse-quarter, follow the word *ghṛtena*, take the genitive case, or be used in the vocative.

The rule regarding all unaccented (anudātta) syllables is an exception; among those [words] such as "pāda" and "vākya," an acute (udātta) accent also exists at the beginning when they function as vocatives, and in cases such as "tiṅ" and "dyāsubādi. 24.

In the Brāhmaṇa, as in the case of a mantra, there is no lowering of voice for an injunction such as "let them not cook," nor for a sentence beginning with "adhaḥ" or "pūrvam," nor for a finite verb following a vocative; however,
if a finite verb were followed by the word "hi," it would be accented with the udātta.
When used in conjunction with the words *net* and *ku*, the first verb is optionally [repeated] (26).

Due to the persistence of the action (*kriyānuṣaṅga*), this is seen even when there is a duplication; likewise elsewhere, there may be a duplication even when there is a distinction between the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the object defined (*lakṣya*), as well as in the case of different actions (*karmaṇām*). (27)

When there is a division of meaning, there is unity of sentence; where [particles] such as *aśanā* do not cause a split, as in "the reason was not destroyed," so too with that which is conveyed by words.
That which is joined with those [words] has no connection with what precedes, nor with what follows.
Just as in the case of "yathā yad dvādaśo dyām," those [words] are subordinate to the sense of the substance; however, some hold that even when separated by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*),
they connect with what precedes the word *tat*, for it is observed that a single [word] can indeed be construed with many.

In a word belonging to the Mādhyaṃdina or Śākala recensions, when an acute (udātta) vowel is followed by grave (anudātta) vowels, those gravis are maintained even in the process of *vivṛtti* (vowelization) and even when separated by consonants (*halvyavāya*), provided they are not followed by an acute vowel. However, because they depend on the original [vowels], their accents are lost even when the *yaṇ* substitutes take their place.

When an acute (udātta) vowel is elided, the resulting grave (nihata) syllable is called the "always-circumflex" (nityasvarita). Furthermore, when two *u* vowels undergo elision and reach a state of oneness within a single word, they are both desired to be acute; however, in other cases, when such a merger occurs, the other [resulting] syllables are otherwise.

In the *Svāyambhuva* [Prātiśākhya], a following *nitya-svarita* is treated as if it were a *kampita* for the sake of meaning; furthermore, even when followed by an acute (*udātta*) vowel, it remains so. A *nitya-svarita* should also be understood as occurring in the case of the root *īṅ*, due to the phonetic combination of syllables (*akṣara-saṃdhi*).

It is threefold: [occurring] at the beginning of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), at the end of a noun (*nāmānta*), and when followed by a case-suffix (*vibhaktau*). (35) It is *sāṃhita* (euphonic) in cases such as *svarvāci*, *vyastaṃ juhu*, and *āsya sūnnīya*;
it is joined (*yukta*) when there is a conjunction with a letter ending in *y* or *v*; and all [other instances] should be understood in the same way. (36)

In words such as *kyātkvala*, the form *nyaṅ* is seen with its hair (*keśa*) shorn; in the case of words beginning with *sub* and so forth, there is the vowel *a* at the end when followed by a non-acute (*anudātta*) vowel. Furthermore, forms such as *sauryodūthya* and *vaidehya* do not arise from two previously unmentioned [suffixes].

Mahyai, meṣyai, bṛhatyai, kuhvāyai, pakā, likewise arādyau, senānye, prapharvyāṃ, gaurī, and am—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras at the end; they consist of three syllables each and are placed at the conclusion of the *syava*. 38–39.
In the words *varṣya* and *bhrātṛvya*, which end in *-ṣya* and do not contain the suffix *iṅ*, the middle syllable is udātta; as for that which is to be (future), it is *āvyam* and *upahavyam*;
for the *dakṣiṇā*, the *suvargādyam* and *divākīrtyam* are not like the preceding [cases].
Thus, having grasped both vigor and lack of vigor, [one should act] toward the sin; 41.
The *anvāhārya* [offering] belongs to the new moon (*amāvāsya*), as does the *kārṣmarya* [wood], but not during a drought;
likewise, the word *ukthya* [is used], and the *ukthya-agra*, the *pārya*, and the *vārya* together in the revealed scripture (*śruti*). 42.
In the *mantre*, *panthi*, *sakthi*, and *duri*, [the final vowel] is sometimes otherwise; [the vowel] of *savyā* is lengthened before *rakṣam*, as is that of *prapathyā* when followed by *paṅkti*.
Likewise, in *rudra*, *ūrmi*, and so forth, [the vowels] are lengthened in *dvandva* compounds, as well as in *meghyā* and *vidyuti*. 43. In *ayoḥ* [the vowel is likewise lengthened].
*kāṭya*, *lipya*, *haritvā*, *ceriṇyānīpya*,
*sikatyayoḥ* (44). At the end of *īṅya*, there are *vāhya*, *grāhya*, *ūhya*, *cāyya*, *grābhya*, *laṃbhya*, *hāryaṃba*, *dhyātavya*, *āvāpya*, *ślokyā*, *taṅkye*, and *devatārdhyam* (45).
The words *tarpyā*, *vṛttyai*, *nikośyābhyām*, and *upādhārya* are subject to avagraha;
as are the words *palvalyā* and *avaṭyā*, and the words *vānyā* and *saṃbhārya*.
The words *jyotiṣyā* and *avyaṃgrahītavyāḥ* are also [subject to avagraha], as are *varūdyā* and *upīcyabarhsvayoḥ*.
*Śīrṣaṇya*, *ūṣmaṇya*, *akarmaṇya*, *amartya*, *apastāvakarya*, and *āvikarya*;
*ūṇya* and *sṛṇya* in the sense of "to be placed upon"; *viśya* in the sense of "belonging to the people"; *āśya*, *bilva*, and *ukhala*;
*niṣṭarkya*, *ārkhya*, and *śikya*; *pākya*, *śīrya*, *ānurya*, *kārya*, and *audarya*. (47–48)

Such are *snāvanī* (vein), *āsanya* (belonging to the mouth), *rājanyā* (royal), *dhānyam* (grain), *kanyā* (maiden), *jaghanyayoḥ* (of the two hind parts), *urvarī* (fertile field), *āyasavātyau* (related to iron and wind), and the two *gavīnyau* (arteries).
(49) [Also] *kaśipavya* (relating to a bed-cover), *ādūtyam* (relating to a messenger), and *hṛdayyayā vadhvā* (with a bride dear to the heart).
One should offer oblations with the *maṇḍūkī* verse for the sake of the thighs; the *śamī* is for the sake of a beautiful body, and the *śruti* is for peace.
One should not occupy [the seat] with a sense of exhaustion; the *kuśyau* is for the two arms, and the *nāyāsya* is likewise for the two shoulders.
The *sādanya* and *sapara* are for the count, as well as for the chariot and compassion. 50–51.
"Even the union with the intermediate tone (nyaṅsvarīyujyam), along with the *sasaumya* and others such as these,
as well as other vowels found in the *Aruṇopaniṣad*, should be understood through study.
Thus ends the fifty vowels.
